fields.problem:
Title: Euler Phi Function by Argument is Injective

Let $f: \N \to \N$ be the [[Definition:Arithmetic Function|arithmetic function]] defined as:
:$\map f n = n \map \phi n$ 
where $\map \phi n$ is the [[Definition:Euler Phi Function|Euler Phi function]] (which is not [[Definition:Injective|injective]]).

Then $f$ is [[Definition:Injective|injective]].
fields.source_context:
0001 | By [[Product of Multiplicative Functions is Multiplicative]] and [[Euler Phi Function is Multiplicative]], $f$ is a [[Definition:Multiplicative Arithmetic Function|multiplicative function]].
0002 | 
0003 | Suppose that $\map f {n_1} = \map f {n_2}$.
0004 | 
0005 | The case $n_1 = 1$ is trivial.
0006 | 
0007 | Let $n_1 > 1$.
0008 | 
0009 | Let $p$ be the largest prime factor of $n_1$.
0010 | 
0011 | By [[Largest Prime Factor of Euler Phi Function]], the largest prime factor of $\map \phi {n_1}$ is less than $p$.
0012 | 
0013 | Thus $p$ is the largest prime factor of $\map f {n_1} = n_1 \map \phi {n_1}$.
0014 | 
0015 | But:
0016 | :$\map f {n_1} = \map f {n_2}$
0017 | 
0018 | Then $p$ is the largest prime factor of $\map f {n_2}$.
0019 | 
0020 | Then $p$ is the largest prime factor of $n_2$.
0021 | {{qed|lemma}}
0022 | 
0023 | Let $p^k$ be the largest power of $p$ dividing $n_1$.
fields.witness: Take n₁ = 4 and p = 2. Then n₁ > 1, and 2 is prime and the largest prime factor of 4. The integers in {1,2,3,4} coprime to 4 are 1 and 3, so φ(4) = 2. Hence the largest prime factor of φ(4) is 2, equal to p rather than strictly less.
